posts.body_html:
It's no secret that Sarracenia leucophylla produces 2 flushes of pitcher growth: one in the spring/early summer, and then the biggest, baddest, most colorful traps during the fall. Now that we have grown out many genetically different variants from throughout it's natural range, it seems like some populations or individuals are capable of producing both nice spring and fall traps, whereas other populations produce small/crappy spring pitchers and amazing fall trap. to make things even more complicated, the same clone that produces crappy pitchers outdoors for us during the early summer can produce amazing early summer traps under greenhouse conditions!

Some years, the white trumpet pitcher plant produces an incredible fall show for us outdoors here in Northern California, whereas during other years, it merely produces phyllodia all year long and then goes dormant. Why does it behave this way?

For the longest time, we speculated it must be temperature. S. leucophylla seems to love warmer temps, and they seem to produce their best pitchers when it's hot. When it's cooler during the summer/early fall, perhaps that prevents the plants from producing fall traps. That hypothesis was thrown out the window when we saw incredible fall pitchers on S. leucophylla Hurricane creek white clone E, grown in Mendocino County, CA. To give you perspective, the average daily summer temperatures up there are in the mid to high 60's. My average daily temperature during the summer here south of San Francisco, CA is roughly 78-80F. To sumarize, S. leucophylla can still produce incredible fall traps with cooler temperatures.

So back to square one. How do you get S. leucophylla to consistently produce fall traps? I still can't answer this question in its entirety as there are multiple factors that contribute to fall trap production. However, I THINK I figured out one important factor: spacing.

What do most S. leucophylla with nice fall traps have in common? Their growth points are getting hit with direct sunlight! IF you pack S. flava tightly together, and the growth points are shaded by surrounding plants, will they stop producing big old traps? Nope. So why is S. leucophylla so much pickier than S. flava? No idea yet.

Here's some observations that suggest light hitting the rhizomes is one factor that determines fall trap production. Photos taken 8/24/15. In the first picture, the tray of S. leucophylla receives direct sunlight to the left and back. Notice the plants in the front, which are shaded and don't receive direct sunlight to the rhizomes, aren't yet producing pitchers. Please note: these plants were recently "pruned" back so now all of the rhizomes can potentially receive light. Before, the leaves were so thick you couldn't see the rhizomes:


Another view: notice plants on the "edge" of the tray, to the left and right, are producing fall traps. everything in the middle and behind are still only producing phyllodia:



Any S. leucophylla grower will become excited when they see this during the fall-the start of the fall pitcher flush:


And some pretty close-ups of the traps:







To be continued with photos of hurricane creek white doing the same thing!

posts.body_html:
I wonder if has something to do with the spike of rainfall we get down here around July/early August. To me, it seems like there's enough rain to keep the plants alive and growing during the spring and summer, and they can even dry out a little in the wild (and maybe this is important). But around late July/early August, it pours almost every afternoon. Maybe this extra water acts as some sort of signal that it's okay to put more energy into producing larger pitchers.

Just a thought.

posts.body_html: I have leuco 'Tarnok' and also one from Garcon Point.  The Tarnok is in a 10 pot, and a huge plant.  It's new fall pitchers are almost 3 feet tall, and has bee going for a while, mature pitchers for the past 3-4 weeks.  The Garcon Point plants, fairly small in size,  are just now starting to get going.  They get the same conditions and light.  I think there must be a combination of light, and light duration that is a trigger.  Her in Tally, we have had hot, wet weather for much of the summer, and no major coolness, or other possible trigge, unless you count cooling to 91 from 97 a big enough drop.

Okay, it's not as obvious anymore with Hurricane creek white, but you can kinda still see what I'm talking about. About 2 weeks ago, I noticed the "front" section of the bed of HCW leucophyllas were in full force, whereas the "back" only had a few traps here and there. The front plants were all well spaced out, and most of the growth points had direct sunlight exposure, whereas plants in the back were way overgrown and very little light was hitting the growth points in the middle of the "patch."

2 weeks ago, I pruned back the HCW plants in the back and even took a few pots out so they could "stretch their legs" and get spaced out even more. Light is now hitting all of the growth points.


Check out how much more densely populated the traps are in the "front" of the bed compared to the back. Same exact clones, same watering, same everything except the plants in the front had significantly more space to grow throughout the season. The growth points of all the plants in the front were getting hit with direct sunlight throughout the majority of the grow season. Photos taken 8/26/15:


Close up of the "front" of the bed:"


Less obvious from this angle, but the "front" of the bed is to the right, and the back is the left. Check out how fall pitcher production in the back (to the left) is a lot less dense:


Check out those new fall traps developing...Ya baby!


And some pretty trap pictures just cuz:


Totally missed taking a pic of this trap when it was in its prime, but here's clone F:

posts.body_html:
This is a great find! Do leucos grow in areas which frequently burn? Maybe they are genetically programmed for feast/famine modes. After an area burns, they go gangbusters and produce a zillion traps, grow their rhizomes nice and fat, and crank out a lot of flowers and seeds.

Once the area gets overgrown again, they flip into survival mode, produce proportionally more phyllodia, and live off the rhizome season after season till the next big burn?

posts.body_html:
Love it Mike! Dang those HCW are siiick! Yeah I speculate that while light and temperature are both important factors for fall pitcher production, light is probably the more critical of the two. In the wild, overgrown, shaded leucos don't tend to pitcher well at all, despite the ambient temperatures being um, hot as F in the fall in their native range. That said, I'm skeptical about dismissing temperature altogether since there seems to be a lot of genetic variation in how different clones respond to temperature under identical lighting conditions (as when they are grown right next to each other in a collection). HCW seem to consistently produce nice spring pitchers in cooler Cali springs (and maybe more capable in cooler fall conditions too?), whereas Alabama - forget about it!
Lastly, just to be super annoying it occurs to me that there is a bit of a confounded relationship between the light and temperature variables. After all, the plants in your trays that get more light also experience a warmer microclimate as a result of getting additional direct solar radiation. Ambient air temps will be the same, but the sun directly striking soil and plant tissue could raise the temps at those more exposed plants significantly. Is this making a difference? I don't know, but it could.
Any way you slice it, I think a leuco getting plenty of light to the whole plant including the rhizome AND experiencing hot temperatures will be a the happiest leuco. Since us growers can't change the weather but we can put our plants in more light, I think you have a point for anyone who's looking to keep their leuco game tight

posts.body_html: I'm just spitballing, but I think photoperiod could play a role too. This could mean either short days or long days are important for fall pitcher production. For example, maybe leucos have a quota for long summer days, and if they hit that quota, they'll put out large fall pitchers. Or similarly, maybe they have a quota for short days, and they need to hit it to put out fall pitchers. And maybe different genotypes have different quotas, so an HCW leuco might have a different quota than a Franklin Co., FL, leuco, for example. This doesn't really explain why, within the Hurricane Creek White genotypes, some produce fall pitchers while others don't, but that's probably where the sunlight and temperature factors come in.

posts.body_html:
Those are great observations, thanks calen and rhizomatus! There's certainly more than just direct sunlight hitting the growth point involved as alluded to earlier in this post. I think the point is that all else being optimal (ie. longer nights, warm day/nights, and full sun, perfect moisture content, lots of energy stored in the rhizome), if you don't get direct light hitting those growth points for a certain period of time, there's less of a chance you'll get fall pitchers.

Genetics also play a huge role. Take these leucophyllas as an example: we have Santa Rosa Co, Walton co, Franklin Co genetics up in this mix, yet compared to hurricane creek white, these plants are way "behind." Some, despite being blasted with full sun on their growth points all season long, are still producing phyllodia today (8/28/15). The pots are kevin BAKIN' in the sun, so the soil is consistently kept warm. Photo taken 8/26/15:



Here's leucophylla AxB select clone Franklin Co, FL. It's producing something in between phyllodia and a fall trap:



Also, just to clarify things, within a population, individuals behave differently. All being equal, some individuals from the same exact bog grown under identical conditions will produce fall pitchers earlier than another individual. And lastly, seedlings behave WAY differently than mature, adult plants.


I took some of my prized leucophylla clones/leuco hybrids and spaced them out quite a bit. This isn't the best experiment since some were already producing fall traps, but it'll be interesting to see if every last plant produces a nice set of fall pitchers. These were spaced out maybe 2 weeks ago, photo taken 8/26/15:



These leucophyllas were jammed packed in community trays, and were transplanted during the middle of July. Might be enough time to establish sufficient roots for nice fall pitchers, but every last rhizome has been getting hit with direct light. Many starting to produce fall pitchers, although these variants produced summer traps all season long. 2 photos below were taken 8/26/15:



From the pic above, a close up of one pot showing the beginning of fall pitchers:




And some pretty trap photos. These are summer traps, which don't look anything close to as amazing as how the fall traps will be. Some of these have solid white throats and the white pigments go down the petiole quite a bit on their fall pitchers:

posts.body_html:
The bed below has been "cleaned up" (there's some photos above before traps were pruned out). To recap, these plants were jam packed in a community tray, so during mid summer (early July?), I transplanted them into individual pots and spaced them out. Every last plant has direct sun hitting the growth point ever since.

Now that it's early September, unlike my overgrown hurricane creek whites, where a few pots sent out zero fall traps and are already dormant, EVERY SINGLE plant below is sending out fall traps! I even did an experiment and transplanted a few in late July to see if I could coax them to produce fall traps by exposing the rhizomes to direct sunlight. Thing is, these had less time to produce roots and acclimate, but interestingly enough, most of the "recently" transplanted individuals are sending out fall traps (although, considering equal sized rhizomes from the same population, the traps produced were smaller than the batch that was transplanted early July).

Long story short, it seems like these plants only need direct light hitting the rhizomes for about a month or so to induce fall traps. For those of us with space issues, this is good news since you don't need to use up too much space for a very long period of time. Of course, timing the spacing is everything, if you space them out during September, it's too late. Perhaps the first week of August is the latest you can wait.



Photos taken 9/7/15:

posts.body_html:
Some updated photos on the experimental leucophylla bed. To recap, I transplanted a bunch of leucophyllas in June and also late july and spaced them such that every last growth point received direct sunlight and wasn't shaded out by neighboring leaves. The results? EVERY SINGLE plant produced fall pitchers, even the smaller, runty plants! They were from 3 different populations, and every plant is genetically unique.

Photos taken 9/27/15. In the front of the first photo, plants were transplanted in late july and are still developing their fall pitchers, but everything in the "back" was transplanted/spaced in June. For the most part, this bed's fall traps have opened and now it seems a lot more full compared to a few weeks ago:


A closer shot. The colors weren't very impressive, and as mentioned before, I believe the plants lose their color from transplanting during the middle of the grow season:


This tub has fully established, huge rhizomes, yet it didn't produce a dense patch of fall pitchers as hoped because the tray was way overgrown and only the growth points on the perimeter received light. Some of the plants that were shaded in the middle still produced fall pitchers, although only one or two at most. I trimmed this entire batch a few weeks before the pitchers produced, so either the growth points received enough light in time, or they're genetically less picky about light hitting the rhizome:
